High flexibility and high bonding — the versatile type
Low flexibility and high bonding — relies on closeness and resistance to change
Moderate flexibility and moderate bonding

rationale.text: PLIANT families feel EMOTIONALLY DISCONNECTED (low bonding) but prefer support from people outside the family and are ABLE to handle stress in a flexible way — shifting roles, making decisions, compromising, and altering family patterns as needed. They are flexible but not emotionally bonded.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: FRAGILE families in the Versatile typology are characterized by:
options: High bonding but low flexibility — rely on closeness and resist change
Lack emotional bonding AND inability to deal with stress in a flexible way
High flexibility and high bonding
Low flexibility and high bonding
Moderate flexibility and moderate bonding

rationale.text: FRAGILE families LACK EMOTIONAL BONDING between members AND are unable to deal with stress in a flexible, participatory way. They are doubly disadvantaged — no closeness AND no adaptability — making them most vulnerable to dysfunction when stress occurs.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: When interviewing a family, you note that all members can say what they want, give input into major decisions, shape rules, and compromise, finding new ways to deal with problems. What type of family is this?
options: Regenerative
Rhythmic
Versatile
Bonded
Durable

rationale.text: This describes a VERSATILE FAMILY — high flexibility AND high bonding. They: say what they want, give input into major decisions, shape rules and practices, compromise, shift responsibilities, and experiment with new ways of dealing with problems and issues.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: INTENTIONAL families in the Rhythmic typology are defined as families that:
options: Neither value nor implement family routines
Value routines and recognize their importance but are unable or unwilling to implement them
Implement family routines rigorously but fail to perceive their value
Have high family time and high valuing of routines
Have no interest in family routines whatsoever

rationale.text: INTENTIONAL families VALUE family routines and RECOGNIZE their importance, but are UNABLE OR UNWILLING to actually implement them. The intention is there, but execution fails. Compare: STRUCTURALIZED families implement routines rigorously but don't perceive their value; UNPATTERNED families neither value nor implement routines.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The Family Life Cycle is BEST described as:
options: A one-time event marking family formation
The normal process of family development involving stressful changes and readjustment
A pathological progression of family dysfunction
A static framework for understanding family structure
An administrative classification system for family types

rationale.text: The Family Life Cycle is the NORMAL PROCESS of family development. It involves a sequence of STRESSFUL CHANGES that require compensating or reciprocal readjustment by the family to maintain viability. Each stage has a developmental task that must be accomplished to proceed to the next stage.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: SECOND ORDER CHANGES in the Family Life Cycle are characterized by:
options: Tasks that must be accomplished within a stage — the 'need to do'
Transformation of an individual's state and meaning
Small adaptations that don't change family structure
Moving to a new residence
Changes in daily routines

rationale.text: SECOND ORDER CHANGES: 'NEED TO BE' — involve TRANSFORMATION of an individual's state and meaning; change in the VERY BASIC ATTRIBUTES of the family system; change in the ROLE AND IDENTITY of family members; occur BETWEEN stages of the Family Life Cycle. Example: when the first child is born, the husband becomes the FATHER and the wife becomes the MOTHER.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: FIRST ORDER CHANGES in the Family Life Cycle are characterized by:
options: Transformation of an individual's identity and role
Tasks accomplished within a stage
Fundamental changes in family structure
Changes that occur between stages
Changes in generational roles

rationale.text: FIRST ORDER CHANGES: 'NEED TO DO' — involve INCREMENTS OF MASTERY AND ADAPTATION; do NOT involve change in the main structure of the family; do NOT involve a change in individual identity; are ADDITIONS to the existing state. Example: a family moving to a new residence — adapting to the new environment without changing who they are.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The KEY PRINCIPLE of the LAUNCHING FAMILY stage is:
options: Accepting parent-offspring separation
Commitment to the new system
Accepting a multitude of entries and exits to the family system
Accepting the shifting of generational goals
Increasing flexibility of boundaries to include children's independence

rationale.text: The LAUNCHING FAMILY key principle: ACCEPTING A MULTITUDE OF ENTRIES AND EXITS to the family system. This stage begins when the FIRST CHILD LEAVES HOME and ends when the LAST CHILD LEAVES HOME. In the Philippines, this is prolonged because unmarried children usually stay with parents.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The KEY PRINCIPLE of the FAMILY WITH ADOLESCENTS stage is:
options: Accepting parent-offspring separation
Commitment to the new system
Accepting marital system to make space for children
Accepting the shifting of generational goals
Increasing flexibility of family boundaries to include children's independence

rationale.text: Family with Adolescents key principle: INCREASING FLEXIBILITY OF FAMILY BOUNDARIES to include children's independence (and grandparent's frailties). This stage starts when the first child reaches adolescent age (12 in the Philippines). Not only teenagers but also parents are undergoing identity crisis at this stage.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: THREE HALLMARKS of the Family with Adolescents stage are:
options: Birth of first child, school enrollment, and puberty
Changes in balance of responsibility with overfunctioning and underfunctioning
Launching of children, empty nest, and retirement
Marriage, birth, and death
Courtship, engagement, and marriage

rationale.text: The THREE HALLMARKS of the Family with Adolescents stage: (1) Changes in the BALANCE OF RESPONSIBILITY along with overfunctioning and underfunctioning; (2) MARKED SHIFTS IN INTENSITY OF RELATIONSHIPS; (3) SURGE OF EXCHANGE WITH THE COMMUNITY AT LARGE. These reflect the adolescent's developmental need for autonomy.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The HONEYMOON STAGE of marriage (0-2 years) is characterized by which emotional issue?
options: Maturing of Relationship
Post-Care Review
Commitment to the marriage
Farewells and Planning
Acceptance of generational shift

rationale.text: The HONEYMOON STAGE (0-2 years): emotional issue = COMMITMENT TO THE MARRIAGE. Critical tasks include: differentiation from family of origin, making room for spouse with family and friends, and adjusting career demands. This is when the couple establishes their identity as a unit.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The MIDDLE MARRIAGE STAGE (10-25 years) is characterized by which emotional issue?
options: Commitment to the marriage
Maturing of Relationship
Post-Care Review
Farewells and Planning
Accepting generational shifts

rationale.text: The MIDDLE MARRIAGE STAGE (10-25 years): emotional issue = POST-CARE REVIEW. Critical tasks include: adjusting to mid-life changes, renegotiating the relationship, and renewing marriage commitment. Parents are often dealing with both adolescent children and aging parents simultaneously during this stage.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The FAMILY IN LATER YEARS stage begins with:
options: The birth of the first grandchild
The departure of the last child from home
The retirement of one or both of the couple
The death of the spouse
The marriage of the first child

rationale.text: The FAMILY IN LATER YEARS: begins with the DEPARTURE OF THE LAST CHILD and continues through retirement of one or both of the couple, ending when both are dead. The key principle is 'accepting the shifting of generational goals' — the middle generation becomes more central.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: Mm and Von are married with a 10-year-old daughter. They reside as an EXTENDED FAMILY with Von's parents. In their present stage of the Family Life Cycle, they should be able to:
options: Increase flexibility of boundaries
Accept parent-offspring separation
Accept marital system to make space for children
Accept shifting of generational goals

rationale.text: With a 10-year-old daughter (young child), they are in the FAMILY WITH YOUNG CHILDREN stage. The key principle is: ACCEPTING MARITAL SYSTEM TO MAKE SPACE FOR CHILDREN. Key tasks include taking on parenting roles and realigning relationships with extended family to include parenting and grandparenting roles.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: For a family in later life, what change in family status is required to proceed developmentally?
options: Development of adult-to-adult relationships between grown-up offspring and their parents
Realignment of relationships with extended families and friends to include the spouse
Realignment of relationships with extended family to include parenting and grandparenting roles
Support for a more central role of middle generation

rationale.text: For Family in Later Years, the 2nd Order Change includes: SUPPORT FOR A MORE CENTRAL ROLE FOR MIDDLE GENERATION. The elderly generation must accept that the middle generation (their adult children) now takes on more central family leadership, while the elderly's role shifts to providing wisdom and experience.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: A 4-year-old female was brought to the clinic with cough and fever. She is an only child; her father is an OFW and her mother is a housewife. What adaptive task does this family face at this stage?
options: Increasing flexibility of family boundaries to include independence of children
Making room in the system for the wisdom and experience of the elderly generation
Pregnancy and childbirth is an important clinical concern
Accepting new members into the system, adopting and developing parenting roles

rationale.text: With a 4-year-old child and an OFW father, this is a FAMILY WITH YOUNG CHILDREN stage. The key 2nd Order Change (adaptive task) = ACCEPTING MARITAL SYSTEM TO MAKE SPACE FOR CHILDREN; TAKING ON PARENTING ROLES. For an OFW family, this also includes realigning roles when a parent is absent.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The UNATTACHED YOUNG ADULT stage has which key principle?
options: Commitment to the new system
Accepting parent-offspring separation
Accepting marital system to make space for children
Increasing flexibility of family boundaries
Accepting the shifting of generational goals

rationale.text: The UNATTACHED YOUNG ADULT stage key principle: ACCEPTING PARENT-OFFSPRING SEPARATION. The young adult has come to terms with the family of origin and formulates personal goals as an individual, including forming a new family. Second-order changes include: differentiation of self in relation to family of origin, development of intimate peer relationships, and establishment of self in work.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: Dealing with gender identity and sexual orientation problems is usually encountered at which stage of the Family Life Cycle?
options: Unattached Young Adult
Family with Young Children
Family with Adolescents
Launching Family

rationale.text: Gender identity and sexual orientation issues typically emerge during the FAMILY WITH ADOLESCENTS stage — this is when adolescents are exploring their identity, including sexual identity. This is listed as one of the common problems encountered during this stage (along with drug abuse, STDs, juvenile delinquency, and suicidal tendencies).

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The 'EMPTINESS SYNDROME' is a common problem associated with which stage of the Family Life Cycle?
options: Family with Young Children
Family with Adolescents
Launching Family
Family in Later Years
Newly Married Couple

rationale.text: The 'EMPTINESS SYNDROME' (empty nest syndrome) is associated with the LAUNCHING FAMILY stage — when children leave home and parents experience feelings of emptiness, purposelessness, and loss of role. Parents may also experience career stagnation, depression, and the burden of over-dependent married children.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The Family Illness Trajectory defines the stages of illness as:
options: Diagnosis, Treatment, Recovery, Death
Onset of Illness, Reaction to Diagnosis
Denial, Anger, Bargaining, Depression, Acceptance
Acute, Subacute, Chronic, Terminal
Pre-symptomatic, Symptomatic, Severe, Critical

rationale.text: The Family Illness Trajectory has FIVE STAGES: (1) ONSET OF ILLNESS; (2) REACTION TO DIAGNOSIS — Impact Phase; (3) MAJOR THERAPEUTIC EFFORTS; (4) RECOVERY PHASE — Early Adjustment to Outcome; (5) ADJUSTMENT TO THE PERMANENCY OF THE OUTCOME. Each stage has specific family and physician roles.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: STAGE I (Onset of Illness) in the Family Illness Trajectory is the stage:
options: When the family starts chemotherapy
When the diagnosis is confirmed
Experienced PRIOR TO CONTACT with health care providers
When the patient is hospitalized
When the family adjusts to a chronic condition

rationale.text: STAGE I is the stage experienced PRIOR TO CONTACT WITH HEALTH CARE PROVIDERS. It is initiated by the warning sign of malaise. Medical beliefs and previous experiences influence the meaning of illness at this stage. The nature of onset (acute vs. gradual) plays an important role in the family's response.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: A 63-year-old father (breadwinner) is finally going home after surgery for colon cancer after almost 1 month. Before giving instructions for home care, you want to check how the family is coping when the patient returns to his former environment. At which stage of the trajectory is the family?
options: Onset of illness
Reaction to diagnosis
Major therapeutic efforts
Early adjustment to outcome

rationale.text: STAGE IV: RECOVERY PHASE — EARLY ADJUSTMENT TO OUTCOME. The patient is returning home after major therapy (surgery). The physician checks how the family is coping with the patient's return — adjusting roles, re-integrating the patient, and adapting to any remaining limitations.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The primary breadwinner of a family suddenly had a stroke, rendering him dependent on a family caregiver. Family members are pointing fingers at each other on who will be caregiver and who will assume the breadwinner role. Nobody can come up with a workable solution. What stage is this?
options: Onset of illness
Reaction to the diagnosis
Major therapeutic efforts
Adjustment to permanency of outcome

rationale.text: STAGE V: ADJUSTMENT TO THE PERMANENCY OF THE OUTCOME. The family is realizing they must ACCEPT and ADJUST to a PERMANENT DISABILITY. The second crisis occurs when the family realizes the pattern they thought was temporary must be accepted as permanent. The inability to reorganize roles signals this stage.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The physician presents the diagnosis to a sobbing patient. The partner is quiet, trying to process everything. The patient asks for the best medication. The family is in which stage?
options: Stage I Onset of Illness
Stage II Impact Phase
Stage III Major Therapeutic Effort
Stage IV Early Adjustment to permanency of the outcome

rationale.text: STAGE II: REACTION TO DIAGNOSIS — IMPACT PHASE. The patient is emotionally reacting (sobbing), the partner is cognitively processing (quiet), and the patient is asking about treatment. These are characteristic of the Impact Phase — emotional response on one plane, cognitive processing on another.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The physician's responsibility in STAGE II (Reaction to Diagnosis) includes all EXCEPT:
options: Making a clinical judgment about the amount of information the patient can absorb given their level of anxiety
Giving small doses of information over time if the diagnosis is particularly traumatic
Exploring the patient's explanatory model of illness
Aid the patient and the family in efficient and functional readjustment
Providing support, continuity of care, and interpreting misunderstood findings

rationale.text: 'Aid the patient and the family in efficient and functional readjustment' is the responsibility in STAGE IV (Recovery Phase), not Stage II. In Stage II, the physician must judge how much information to give, give information in doses, provide support, and interpret misunderstood findings.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In the COGNITIVE PLANE of Stage II (Reaction to Diagnosis), PHASE IV represents:
options: Initial tension and confusion with lack of capacity for problem solving
Repeated failure in deriving the diagnosis leading to exacerbation of tension
Increasing assessment and receptivity to new approaches for relief of distress
Eventual acceptance of diagnosis enabling them to mobilize resources and recognize the family

rationale.text: COGNITIVE PLANE Phase IV: EVENTUAL ACCEPTANCE OF DIAGNOSIS enables the family to MOBILIZE RESOURCES and REORGANIZE the family. The quality of family reorganization at this phase determines if they achieve healthy adaptation or reorganize at a more dysfunctional level.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The HOSPITALIZATION of the MOTHER has which specific impact according to the Family Illness Trajectory?
options: Represents the special economic burden on the family
Poses the GREATEST IMPACT on other family members and highest risk of family dysfunction
Creates a special syndrome of emotional problems — hostility and abandonment
Makes them vulnerable to fears of death, rejection, abandonment, and loneliness
Causes helplessness, guilt, frustration, or hurt

rationale.text: When the MOTHER is hospitalized: GREATEST IMPACT on other family members + HIGHEST RISK OF FAMILY DYSFUNCTION. The mother typically manages household and caregiving roles, so her absence disrupts the entire family system most severely.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: For TERMINAL ILLNESS, the initial response in diagnosis is of:
options: Acceptance and planning
Shock and overwhelming anxiety, as they respond to the pain with denial
Anger and bargaining
Depression and withdrawal
Relief that the problem is identified

rationale.text: For TERMINAL ILLNESS: the initial response is SHOCK AND OVERWHELMING ANXIETY. As they respond to the pain with DENIAL. If the family is functional, members draw close together to provide care and support. If dysfunctional, this can be the seed for future family discord and breakdown.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: Nataniel, 46/M, is diagnosed with Stage IV pancreatic cancer. He decides not to undergo chemotherapy and desires to just stay at home. The family must do the following during this stage:
options: Choose a therapeutic plan appropriate for the patient
Accept and adjust to the permanency of the patient's illness
Maintain hope that the patient will return to full health
Believe that this phase is only temporary and will resolve in time

rationale.text: STAGE V: ADJUSTMENT TO THE PERMANENCY OF THE OUTCOME. With terminal cancer refusing chemotherapy and choosing home care, the family must ACCEPT AND ADJUST to the PERMANENCY of the illness outcome. The whole family must give up hope for full return to health and accept that life must go forward with this new reality.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The FAMILY APGAR was originally described by Smilkstein and assesses:
options: Family genetic history and hereditary diseases
Adaptation, Partnership, Growth, Affection, and Resolve
Social, Cultural, Religious, Economic, Educational, and Medical factors
Family relationships and interaction patterns
Community resources and social support networks

rationale.text: The Family APGAR (Smilkstein) is a rapid screening instrument for FAMILY DYSFUNCTION measuring the individual's level of SATISFACTION about family relationships. It has 5 items: (A) Adaptation, (P) Partnership, (G) Growth, (A) Affection, (R) Resolve. Scores: 8-10 = highly functional, 4-7 = moderately dysfunctional, 0-3 = severely dysfunctional.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In the Family APGAR, 'RESOLVE' refers to:
options: How the family adapts to stress by using internal and external resources
How the family communicates and shares decision-making
Both physical and emotional growth and the freedom to change
The satisfaction with how emotions are shared between members
How time, space, money are shared

rationale.text: RESOLVE = how TIME, SPACE, and MONEY are SHARED. It measures members' SATISFACTION WITH THE COMMITMENT made by other members of the family. For example, 'I am satisfied with the way my family and I share time together.'

subject: Family & Community Health
question: 'PARTNERSHIP' in the Family APGAR refers to:
options: The capability of the family to utilize and share inherent resources
The SHARING OF DECISION-MAKING
Both physical and emotional growth
How emotions like love, anger, and hatred are shared between members
How time, space, money are shared

rationale.text: PARTNERSHIP = SHARING OF DECISION-MAKING. It measures the satisfaction attained in solving problems by COMMUNICATING. For example, 'I am satisfied with the way my family talks over things with me and shares problems with me.'

subject: Family & Community Health
question: A patient scores: A=2, P=1, G=2, A=1, R=0. Total = 6. The Family APGAR interpretation is:
options: Highly functional family (8-10)
Moderately dysfunctional family (4-7)
Severely dysfunctional family (0-3)
Functional family
Normal family

rationale.text: Total score = 6 = MODERATELY DYSFUNCTIONAL FAMILY (4-7 points). Note the lowest score is in R (Resolve = time sharing), suggesting dissatisfaction with how the family shares time together. This warrants further family assessment.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The FAMILY CIRCLE TECHNIQUE is described as:
options: A genogram with 3 generations
A brief, graphic method for disclosing, gathering
A tool that measures satisfaction with family functioning
A mapping tool for community resources
A scoring system for family dysfunction

rationale.text: The FAMILY CIRCLE: a brief, graphic method where the physician draws a LARGE CIRCLE and instructs the patient to draw SMALLER CIRCLES representing themselves and all important people. People can be inside or outside, touching or far apart, large or small depending on significance. Through this tool, one can assess openness, boundaries, support, function, triangulation, and interdependence.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: SCREEM is an acronym standing for:
options: Social, Cultural, Religious, Economic, Educational, and Medical factors
Support, Coherence, Resilience, Empathy, Empowerment, and Mobility
Social, Cultural, Relational, Economic, Environmental, and Medical
Safety, Cohesion, Resilience, Education, Employment, and Medical
Strengths, Challenges, Resources, Evaluation, Education, and Management

rationale.text: SCREEM = Social, Cultural, Religious, Economic, Educational, and Medical factors affecting health. It assesses the family's capacity to participate in provision of health care or to cope with crisis. Each factor can be a RESOURCE (strength) or PATHOLOGY (weakness/barrier) for the family.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: SCREEM is MOST commonly used when:
options: A new patient is enrolled in a family health care program
The need for care is long or lasts a lifetime
A patient has a minor acute illness
Conducting a routine annual physical examination
A patient is being discharged from the hospital

rationale.text: SCREEM is most commonly used when the NEED FOR CARE IS LONG OR LASTS A LIFETIME — such as in chronically-ill, terminally-ill, and hospice care patients. It identifies what resources the family has (social support, financial capacity, education, medical access) and what barriers (pathologies) exist.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The FAMILY GENOGRAM must consist of at least how many generations?
options: 3 or more

rationale.text: The Family Genogram must consist of 3 OR MORE GENERATIONS, each identified by Roman numerals. The first-born of each generation is farthest to the left, with siblings following to the right in order of birth. It serves three purposes: overview of interrelationships, looking at medical/psychosocial problems, and understanding multigenerational family systems.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The INDEX PATIENT (proband) in a Family Genogram is:
options: The oldest family member
The family member with the most serious disease
One member of greater medical significance because of an illness
The family member who initiated the consultation
The physician conducting the assessment

rationale.text: The INDEX PATIENT (proband) is the family member of GREATER MEDICAL SIGNIFICANCE because of an illness, identified with an ARROW on the genogram. Persons living in the same household are enclosed with a heavy line. Significant diseases are illustrated using symbols that must appear in the legend.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The FAMILY ECOMAP is BEST described as:
options: A graphic representation of family structure through 3 generations
A pictorial representation of patients' environment and the quality of each interaction
A tool measuring satisfaction with family relationships
A scoring system for family dysfunction
A genogram of family medical history

rationale.text: The ECOMAP is a PICTORIAL REPRESENTATION of the elements of the patient's environment and the NATURE AND QUALITY OF INTERACTIONS between those elements. It illustrates 3 dimensions for each connection: STRENGTH (weak, tenuous, strong), IMPACT (draining or providing resources), and QUALITY (stressful or not stressful).

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In Minuchin's Family Map, ENMESHMENT is characterized by:
options: Boundaries that are too rigid, causing emotional distance between members
Members being overly reactive to stress on one member and demonstrating a lack of individual autonomy
A third person being drawn into a two-person system to diffuse anxiety
Two members 'siding' with each other against a third
Members being emotionally distant and unresponsive to each other

rationale.text: ENMESHMENT occurs when boundaries are DIFFUSE — parents have no privacy from children, members are OVERLY REACTIVE to stress on one member, and there is LACK OF INDIVIDUAL AUTONOMY. When families care for young children, high enmeshment is appropriate; but at later life cycle stages, it can inhibit individual development.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: TRIANGULATION in family dynamics occurs when:
options: Three family members have equal authority
A third person is drawn into a two-person system to diffuse anxiety or conflict
Three generations live together
Three family members form a coalition against one
Two members have a rigid boundary between them

rationale.text: TRIANGULATION: a third person is drawn into a TWO-PERSON SYSTEM to DIFFUSE ANXIETY OR CONFLICT. Example: rather than arguing with each other about marital issues, parents express their discontent by arguing over parenting their son. The son (third person) is triangulated by the parents' conflict.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In Minuchin's Family Map, DISENGAGEMENT is characterized by:
options: Diffuse boundaries and over-involvement
Boundaries that are too rigid
A third person being drawn into a two-person conflict
Two members forming an alliance against a third
Members having no individual boundaries

rationale.text: DISENGAGEMENT: characterized by boundaries that are TOO RIGID — members are EMOTIONALLY DISTANT and UNRESPONSIVE to each other. Example: a husband who does not tell his wife or children about any of his health problems. The mother-child subsystem that excludes the father's involvement in parenting is also disengagement.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The FAMILY LIFELINE is MOST useful when:
options: Assessing a patient's level of satisfaction with family relationships
Anticipating a long-term illness, difficult caregiving
Mapping community resources and social support
Identifying hereditary diseases in the family
Conducting routine annual family assessments

rationale.text: The FAMILY LIFELINE is most useful when ANTICIPATING A LONG-TERM ILLNESS, the presence of DIFFICULT CAREGIVING, or NON-ADHERENCE TO TREATMENT. It summarizes the family's significant experiences chronologically, helps process family flexibility when dealing with changes, and includes both normative and non-normative crises.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The SCREEM-RES scoring interprets a score of 7-12 as:
options: Adequate family resources (13-18)
Moderately inadequate family resources
Severely inadequate family resources (0-6)
Highly dysfunctional family
Normal family resources

rationale.text: SCREEM-RES scoring: 13-18 = ADEQUATE family resources; 7-12 = MODERATELY INADEQUATE family resources; 0-6 = SEVERELY INADEQUATE family resources. Lower scores indicate the family has fewer resources to cope with illness and provide care, requiring more external support and intervention.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The DRAW-A-FAMILY TEST (DRAFT) is classified as:
options: A quantitative assessment tool with standardized scoring
A projective technique providing clues on family members' personalities
A tool exclusively for children under 12
A screening tool for genetic diseases in the family
A structured interview technique

rationale.text: DRAFT is a PROJECTIVE TECHNIQUE that: provides clues on individual family members' personalities AND serves as a diagnostic device. Family members draw their family, revealing unconscious dynamics. Drawings are first to show incipient psychopathology and the last to lose signs of illness after recovery. Interpretation is made by a Clinical Psychologist.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: Mang Krenz, 65/M, was diagnosed with mature cataract on both eyes. He cannot afford the operation and feels he cannot ask help from his children. Which aspect of the Family APGAR is compromised?
options: Adaptation
Partnership
Growth
Affection
Resolve

rationale.text: ADAPTATION = the capability of the family to UTILIZE AND SHARE INHERENT RESOURCES (intra-familial or extra-familial). Mang Krenz cannot turn to his family for help (financial resources) when something is troubling him — this is the ADAPTATION component of the APGAR.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: A patient's APGAR score is: A-almost always (2), P-some of the time (1), G-almost always (2), A-almost always (2), R-almost always (2). Total = 9. This is a:
options: Severely dysfunctional family (0-3)
Moderately dysfunctional family (4-7)
Highly functional family (8-10)
Normal family
Dysfunctional family

rationale.text: Total score = 9 = HIGHLY FUNCTIONAL FAMILY (8-10 points). All components score well except Partnership (sharing of decision-making and communication about problems) which scores 'some of the time.' This would warrant gentle exploration of communication patterns in the family.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In Smilkstein's Cycle of Family Function, when extra-familial resources are INADEQUATE, the family goes into:
options: Adaptation
Functional equilibrium
Crisis → Maladaptation using pathologic defense mechanisms
Terminal disequilibrium
Regeneration

rationale.text: In Smilkstein's cycle: Stressful life event → Disequilibrium. If family resources are adequate → Adaptation → Functional equilibrium. If inadequate → CRISIS. If extra-familial resources are adequate → Adaptation. If extra-familial resources are ALSO inadequate → MALADAPTATION using pathologic defense mechanisms (denial, repression, somatization, projection) → Terminal disequilibrium or Pathologic equilibrium.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The FAMILY MAP (Minuchin) uses which symbols for boundaries?
options: Solid lines for clear, dotted lines for rigid, and broken lines for diffuse
Clear, Rigid, Diffuse
Arrows for clear, brackets for rigid, waves for diffuse
Roman numerals for clear boundaries and Arabic numerals for diffuse
Triangles for enmeshment and squares for disengagement

rationale.text: Minuchin's Family Map boundary symbols: CLEAR = dashed line (- - - - ); RIGID = solid line (———); DIFFUSE = dotted line (. . . . . . .). Clear boundaries prevent interference but allow contact; rigid boundaries lead to disengagement; diffuse boundaries lead to enmeshment.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The Active Listening Skills mnemonic ABLe-ReP stands for:
options: Acknowledge, Believe, Listen, Respond, Provide
Attending, Bracketing, Leading, Reflecting, Probing
Accept, Bracket, Learn, Reflect, Pause
Attend, Balance, Lead, Respond, Plan
Assess, Bracket, Listen, Reflect, Probe

rationale.text: ABLe-ReP = Attending, Bracketing, Leading, Reflecting (Content, Feeling, Experience), Probing. These are the 5 active listening skills from Carl Rogers' humanistic client-centered counseling model. They turn a biomedical consult into a biopsychosocial one.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: BRACKETING as an active listening skill is:
options: A verbal skill for summarizing what the patient says
Setting aside our biases and pre-conceived notions to listen without judgment
A technique for organizing information from the patient
A method for asking probing questions
A way to maintain eye contact with the patient

rationale.text: BRACKETING is primarily a MENTAL SKILL (not verbal or non-verbal). It means SETTING ASIDE our biases, prejudices, and pre-conceived notions to make way for what the patient is REALLY saying. When a patient shares alternative treatment choices, bracketing allows the physician to listen without judgment.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The ATTENDING skills mnemonic LOVERS stands for:
options: Look, Observe, Voice, Engage, Relax, Sit
Leaning forward, Open stance/posture, Voice of empathy/compassion
Listen, Open, Validate, Empathize, Respond, Support
Look, Open, Voice, Empower, Relax, Silence
Lean, Observe, Voice, Express, Reassure, Sit

rationale.text: LOVERS = Leaning forward, Open stance/posture, Voice of empathy/compassion, Eye contact, Relaxed setting, Sit at an angle (45°). These are the NONVERBAL attending skills that communicate 'I am listening to you / I am paying attention' without words.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: REFLECTING EXPERIENCE (active listening skill) involves:
options: Summarizing what the patient said in fewer words
Naming the emotion the patient is feeling
Verbalizing nonverbal cues given by the patient
Using open-ended questions to elicit more information
Setting aside biases to listen without judgment

rationale.text: REFLECTING EXPERIENCE = verbalizing the NONVERBAL CUES given by the patient. These cues are UNCONSCIOUS and are valuable clues to emotions. Example: 'I noticed that a while ago, you looked out at the door at your wife then you shut it. Could you tell me what was behind that action?'

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In the CEA method, the EDUCATION step addresses:
options: Teaching the patient about anatomy and physiology
Emotionally Critical Misperceptions
Prescribing medications based on evidence
Developing an action plan for the patient
Conducting a family meeting

rationale.text: EDUCATION in CEA addresses EMOTIONALLY CRITICAL MISPERCEPTIONS (ECMs) — the misperceptions causing the GREATEST EMOTIONAL UPSET. The ECM is addressed FIRST (before pathophysiology and pharmacology) because the patient is distracted by emotions. Explanations must be in the patient's language — simple, avoiding scientific jargon.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In the SPIKES protocol, what does 'P' (Perception) represent?
options: Preparing the physician psychologically for breaking bad news
Assessing what the patient already knows or understands about their condition
Presenting the prognosis to the patient
Planning the follow-up appointments
Providing written information to the patient

rationale.text: P = PERCEPTION: 'BEFORE YOU TELL, ASK.' Use open-ended questions to assess the patient's current understanding of their medical situation. Establish what the patient already knows or expects. This helps tailor how the bad news is delivered and can also serve as a 'warning shot.'

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In the SPIKES protocol, 'K' (Knowledge) involves:
options: Asking what the patient wants to know
Assessing the patient's current understanding
Warning the patient that bad news is coming
Setting up the interview in a private room
Empathizing with the patient's emotions

rationale.text: K = KNOWLEDGE: GIVING INFORMATION. This involves: warning the patient bad news is coming, starting at the patient's level of comprehension and vocabulary, using non-technical words, avoiding excessive bluntness, and giving information in SMALL CHUNKS, periodically checking for understanding. Allow pauses for the patient to digest.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The NURSE model for empathy in the SPIKES protocol stands for:
options: Name, Understand, Respond, Support, Evaluate
Name, Understand, Respect, Support, Explore
Normalize, Understand, Reflect, Support, Empower
Name, Uncover, Reassure, Support, Examine
Normalize, Understand, Respond, Strengthen, Explore

rationale.text: NURSE = Name ('I imagine this must be upsetting' — name the emotion), Understand ('I expect most people would feel that way in a situation like this'), Respect ('I'm impressed with how well you've handled such a tough situation'), Support ('I'll be here to help you through this'), Explore ('Tell me more about how you're feeling and what this means for you').

subject: Family & Community Health
question: Which LEVEL OF PHYSICIAN INVOLVEMENT WITH FAMILIES involves systematic family assessment and planned intervention, requiring background knowledge of Family Systems Theory?
options: Level 1
Level 2
Level 3
Level 4
Level 5

rationale.text: LEVEL 4: SYSTEMATIC FAMILY ASSESSMENT AND PLANNED INTERVENTION. Physicians have background knowledge of Family Systems Theory, should be skilled enough to assess family functions and carry out short-term family-level interventions. Uses Rogerian counseling and some forms of cognitive behavior therapy. Requires DIPLOMATE level training.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The MOST APPROPRIATE degree of involvement with MOST families is:
options: Levels 1 and 2
Levels 2 and 3
Levels 3 and 4
Levels 4 and 5
Level 5 only

rationale.text: The MOST APPROPRIATE degree of involvement with most families is LEVELS 2 AND 3. Level 2: providing ongoing medical information and advice. Level 3: eliciting feelings and providing emotional support (CEA model). Level 4 requires more intensive training; Level 5 (Family Therapy) is beyond the scope of family practice.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: A physician who focuses on the biomedical problem, has a busy practice due to time pressure, and uses one-way communication with families is at which level of physician involvement?
options: Level 1
Level 2
Level 3
Level 4
Level 5

rationale.text: LEVEL 1: MINIMAL EMPHASIS ON THE FAMILY. Physicians at this level consider dealing with families as necessary only for practical and medico-legal reasons. They focus on the BIOMEDICAL PROBLEM and ONE-WAY COMMUNICATION prevails. They are typically physicians with very busy clinical practices owing to time pressure.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: A family physician conducts a family meeting for a patient with cervical cancer using the CEA model to assess and manage psychosocial factors. This is what level of physician involvement?
options: Level 1
Level 2
Level 3
Level 4

rationale.text: LEVEL 3: ELICITING FEELINGS AND PROVIDING EMOTIONAL SUPPORT. Key features: meeting with families, providing information and medical advice, responding to emotional needs, supporting the psychosocial impact of illness, and using the CATHARSIS-EDUCATION-ACTION (CEA) model for individual health education.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The 'S' (Setting) in the SPIKES protocol for breaking bad news requires:
options: Sending an email to prepare the patient
Standing at the patient's bedside in the hospital corridor
A private, comfortable, quiet room where the physician and patient are sitting
Conducting the disclosure over the telephone
Involving all available hospital staff

rationale.text: SETTING: arrange for PRIVACY (never break bad news standing in a corridor!), involve significant others, SIT DOWN (both physician and patient), maintain eye contact, manage time constraints (turn off beepers/phones), have tissues available, and arrange chairs at approximately 45° angles to avoid physical barriers between physician and patient.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: Community Oriented Primary Care (COPC) is BEST defined as:
options: A strategy exclusively for urban health centers
A strategy combining primary health care and community medicine in practice
A program for specialist physician training
An emergency response framework for infectious diseases
A hospital-based quality improvement program

rationale.text: COPC (Abramson and Kark) = a strategy whereby elements of PRIMARY HEALTH CARE and COMMUNITY MEDICINE are SYSTEMATICALLY DEVELOPED and BROUGHT TOGETHER in a COORDINATED PRACTICE. It unifies clinical care of individuals with community medicine — using both epidemiologic and clinical skills as complementary functions.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The FIVE ESSENTIAL FEATURES of COPC are:
options: Accessibility, Comprehensiveness, Coordination, Continuity, and Accountability
Use of epidemiologic and clinical skills as complementary functions, defined population, defined programs, community involvement
Community diagnosis, intervention planning, implementation, evaluation, and re-assessment
Primary care, secondary care, tertiary care, prevention, and rehabilitation
Doctors, nurses, pharmacists, social workers, and community health workers

rationale.text: The 5 ESSENTIAL FEATURES of COPC: (1) Use of EPIDEMIOLOGIC AND CLINICAL SKILLS as complementary functions; (2) DEFINED POPULATION as target; (3) DEFINED PROGRAMS to deal with community health problems; (4) INVOLVEMENT OF THE COMMUNITY in promoting its health; (5) ACCESSIBILITY — not just geographic but free from fiscal, social, cultural, and communication barriers.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The 6 STEPS OF COPC (Chen et al.) are:
options: Plan, Do, Check, Act, Evaluate, Reassess
Define and Characterize the Community, Prioritization, Detailed Assessment
Survey, Diagnosis, Intervention, Monitoring, Evaluation, Modification
Community Diagnosis, Planning, Implementation, Monitoring, Evaluation, Decision-making
Define, Diagnose, Design, Deliver, Document, Decide

rationale.text: The 6 STEPS: (1) DEFINE AND CHARACTERIZE the community; (2) PRIORITIZATION of health problems; (3) DETAILED ASSESSMENT of the selected health problem; (4) INTERVENTION PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION; (5) MONITORING; (6) EVALUATION AND RE-ASSESSMENT. COPC is a continuous cycle.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In COPC, the CARDINAL MEMBERS of the health team include:
options: Administrators, laboratory staff, pharmacy, secretarial workers
Physicians, nurses, social case workers, and community organizers/health educators
Epidemiologists, biostatisticians, sociologists
Specialists and hospital consultants only
Government officials and community leaders

rationale.text: CENTRAL/NUCLEAR MEMBERS of the COPC team: PHYSICIANS, NURSES, SOCIAL CASE WORKERS, and COMMUNITY ORGANIZERS/HEALTH EDUCATORS. SUPPORTIVE MEMBERS include: administrators, laboratory, pharmacy, secretarial, and health records. CONSULTATIVE MEMBERS include: epidemiologists, biostatisticians, and medical sociologists.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In COPC, 'PRIORITIZATION' of health problems should involve the community and use mutually agreed upon criteria such as:
options: The most expensive conditions to treat
Severity of the health problem and prevalence among the defined population
The physician's personal interest in specific conditions
Conditions required by government programs
The most recent health trends from international reports

rationale.text: PRIORITIZATION criteria (mutually agreed upon with the community): SEVERITY (morbidity and mortality) of the health problem + PREVALENCE among the defined population. Because of limited resources, the COPC team must choose ONE problem to focus on. Prioritization INVOLVES THE COMMUNITY — it cannot be imposed by health professionals alone.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The COMMUNITY in COPC may be defined as (in order of preference):
options: Only geographic communities in rural areas
A 'true' community, a defined neighborhood
Only patients who use the health center
Only indigenous communities
Only urban communities

rationale.text: In COPC, the 'community' (in order of preference): (1) a 'true' sociological community; (2) a defined neighborhood; (3) workers in a factory/students in a school; (4) people registered as potential users of a health service; (5) users/repeated users of a defined service. The term is broad and not limited to 'true' communities.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: In the complementary functions of clinical and epidemiologic skills in COPC, the EPIDEMIOLOGIC equivalent of 'Continuing Observation' of a patient is:
options: Treatment
Community health diagnosis
Survey
Continuing surveillance of health state of the community
Intervention

rationale.text: Clinical 'Continuing Observation' (evaluation of patient's progress) → Epidemiologic 'CONTINUING SURVEILLANCE' (surveillance of health state of community and ensuring continuing action, evaluation of intervention programs). Clinical skills focus on individuals; epidemiologic skills focus on population groups.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: You identify that hypertension and diabetes are the prevalent non-communicable diseases in the community. Which COPC step is being reflected?
options: Intervention planning
Community health diagnosis and health surveillance
Implementation
Evaluation

rationale.text: Identifying hypertension and diabetes as the PREVALENT health problems in the community represents COMMUNITY HEALTH DIAGNOSIS AND HEALTH SURVEILLANCE. This step requires epidemiologic study of the differential distribution of particular health conditions and the factors that determine their distribution.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: Which of the following is considered an ABSOLUTE ESSENTIAL feature of COPC?
options: Ability of health team to physically go out into the community
Integration of curative and promotive health care
Involvement of the community in the promotion of its health
Multidisciplinary health team
Mobility of the health team

rationale.text: INVOLVEMENT OF THE COMMUNITY in the promotion of its health is an ABSOLUTE ESSENTIAL feature of COPC. Community involvement may be seen as a PREREQUISITE for the satisfactory and continued functioning of a COPC service. Multidisciplinary team and mobility are DESIRABLE but not essential features.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The PROCESSES IN THE DEVELOPMENT OF COPC include all EXCEPT:
options: Preliminary steps
Community health diagnosis and health surveillance
Planning of intervention
Promoting community involvement

rationale.text: The established COPC development processes: Preliminary steps; Community health diagnosis and health surveillance; Planning of intervention; Implementation; Evaluation; Decision making for future action. 'PROMOTING COMMUNITY INVOLVEMENT' per se is not listed as a separate PROCESS — it is embedded throughout all processes, but it is not a standalone step in the classic framework.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: The five attributes ESSENTIAL TO THE PRACTICE OF GOOD PRIMARY CARE (Institute of Medicine) include:
options: Diagnosis, Treatment, Prevention, Rehabilitation, Palliation
Accessibility, Comprehensiveness, Coordination, Continuity, and Accountability
Quality, Safety, Effectiveness, Efficiency, Equity
Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, Quaternary, Quinary
Biomedical, Psychosocial, Cultural, Environmental, Spiritual

rationale.text: The Institute of Medicine's 5 essential attributes of good primary care: (1) ACCESSIBILITY; (2) COMPREHENSIVENESS; (3) COORDINATION; (4) CONTINUITY; (5) ACCOUNTABILITY. Note: the PHC 5Cs are similar but slightly different — First Contact, Comprehensiveness, Coordination, Continuity, Person-Centeredness.

subject: Family & Community Health
question: COPC is meant to be practiced as a CONTINUOUS CYCLE. After a successful intervention is in place to address one issue, the cycle can begin again at which step?
options: Define and Characterize the Community — start completely over
Prioritization stage — to choose a new health problem
Detailed Assessment — gathering more data
Evaluation — to continue evaluating the same problem
Intervention Planning — to modify the existing intervention

rationale.text: Once a successful intervention is in place, COPC cycles back to the PRIORITIZATION STAGE to choose a NEW health problem. The definition and characterization generally remain appropriate for some time with only intermittent updates. COPC is a CONTINUOUS CYCLE — there is always a next health problem to address.
